The question of whether sex education should be taught in schools is genuinely contested, with most retrieved evidence supporting it but some sources presenting opposing views and contradictory research. The majority of sources argue strongly in favor: research cited by the Journal of Adolescent Health shows that comprehensive sex education leads to safer choices, fewer unplanned pregnancies, and better protection against STIs [d4], and studies show states with abstinence-only education have higher pregnancy and STI rates than those with comprehensive programs [d6]. Comprehensive, culturally responsive sex education has also been shown to help prevent intimate partner violence, reduce sexual risk behaviors, and support healthy relationship development [d2], while also building social-emotional skills, reducing bullying, and preventing child sexual abuse [d1]. However, d7 presents a directly opposing viewpoint, citing a 2002 Journal of Health Economics study that found "some evidence that greater access to contraception is associated with an increase in underage conceptions," and arguing that schools have no right to override parental authority on sexual matters and that "children don't need sex ed, they need chastity ed" [d7]. The debate is further complicated by the distinction between comprehensive sex education and abstinence-only programs, with advocates on both sides, and by the fact that only 13–18 states require sex education content to be medically accurate, leaving wide variation in what is actually taught [d4][d2][d3].
